member.name: P:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.Models.SqliteConcurrencyOptions.MaxRetryAttempts
member.summary: The maximum number of retry attempts when an operation fails with SQLITE_BUSY or SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT.
member.remarks: Each retry uses exponential backoff with jitter starting at 100 ms. Must be greater than zero. Default is 3.

member.name: P:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.Models.SqliteConcurrencyOptions.BusyTimeout
member.summary: Per-connection busy timeout passed to PRAGMA busy_timeout. SQLite will automatically retry lock acquisition for up to this duration before returning SQLITE_BUSY.

remarks.para: This is the first layer of busy handling. The library also adds application-level retry with jitter (the second layer) because SQLite may bypass the busy handler to avoid deadlocks — for example, when a read transaction attempts to upgrade to a write transaction.
Must be non-negative. A value of disables the built-in handler and relies entirely on the application-level retry. Default is 30 seconds.

member.name: P:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.Models.SqliteConcurrencyOptions.CommandTimeout
member.summary: EF Core command timeout (seconds) applied via SqliteDbContextOptionsBuilder.CommandTimeout.
member.remarks: Must be non-negative. Default is 300 (5 minutes).

member.name: P:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.Models.SqliteConcurrencyOptions.WalAutoCheckpoint
member.summary: Number of WAL frames after which SQLite automatically runs a passive checkpoint (PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint).

remarks.para: A lower value keeps the WAL file small (reducing read overhead) but adds more checkpoint I/O. A higher value reduces checkpoint frequency at the cost of a larger WAL file and potential read slowdown as readers must scan more frames.
Must be non-negative. Set to 0 to disable automatic checkpointing (manual checkpoints only via PRAGMA wal_checkpoint). Default is 1000 pages (~4 MB at the default 4 096-byte page size).

member.name: P:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.Models.SqliteConcurrencyOptions.SynchronousMode
member.summary: Controls how aggressively SQLite flushes commits to stable storage (PRAGMA synchronous).

remarks.para: Default: — recommended for WAL mode. The database is always consistent after an application crash. A power failure or OS crash may roll back the last committed transaction(s) that had not yet been checkpointed.
Use or when power-loss durability is critical. Be aware that these settings significantly increase write latency due to additional fsync calls on every commit.

member.name: P:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.Models.SqliteConcurrencyOptions.UpgradeTransactionsToImmediate
member.summary: When (the default), the interceptor rewrites plain BEGIN and BEGIN TRANSACTION commands to BEGIN IMMEDIATE.

remarks.para: BEGIN IMMEDIATE acquires a reserved write lock at transaction start, guaranteeing that no later statement in the transaction will fail with SQLITE_BUSY before commit. This eliminates the common failure mode where a deferred transaction (plain BEGIN) successfully reads data but then fails with SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT on the first write because another writer committed in the meantime.

Trade-off: Upgrading read-only transactions to IMMEDIATE acquires an unnecessary write lock, which can reduce concurrency slightly when many read-only operations run simultaneously. If your application exclusively uses explicit read-only transactions and manages write transactions manually, set this to and start write transactions with BEGIN IMMEDIATE yourself.
Commands that already contain IMMEDIATE or EXCLUSIVE are never modified.

member.name: P:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.Models.SqliteConcurrencyOptions.WriteQueueCapacity
member.summary: Bounded capacity of the per-database write queue.

remarks.para: When set, the write queue uses a bounded with BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait. Callers that enqueue writes while the channel is at capacity will wait asynchronously until space is available, providing explicit back-pressure under heavy write load.
When (the default), the channel is unbounded and callers are never delayed by back-pressure. The underlying queue still serializes writes in FIFO order; only the maximum depth is unrestricted.
This value is used only when the write queue is first created for a given database. Changing it after first use has no effect.

member.name: T:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.Models.SqliteSynchronousMode
member.summary: Controls how aggressively SQLite flushes write operations to stable storage (PRAGMA synchronous).

remarks.para: The right choice depends on your durability requirements and workload:

list.item: For WAL mode (the default), is almost always correct. Commits are durable against application crashes; the small risk is losing the last transaction or two after an unexpected power loss or OS crash.
For rollback journal mode, or provides stronger guarantees at the cost of more fsync calls per commit.
trades all durability for maximum speed and is only appropriate for ephemeral or fully-reproducible databases.

remarks.para: See the SQLite documentation for the complete specification.

member.name: F:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.Models.SqliteSynchronousMode.Off
member.summary:
PRAGMA synchronous = OFF — SQLite hands off writes to the OS and continues without waiting for any flush. Maximum performance.
Risk: A power failure or OS crash at any point can corrupt the database. Not recommended for production data.

member.name: F:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.Models.SqliteSynchronousMode.Normal
member.summary:
PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL — SQLite syncs at WAL checkpoint boundaries rather than on every commit.
The database is always consistent after an application crash. A power failure or OS crash may roll back the last one or two transactions that had been committed by the application but not yet checkpointed.
This is the recommended setting for WAL mode and the library default. It delivers significantly higher write throughput than while providing acceptable durability for most workloads.

member.name: F:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.Models.SqliteSynchronousMode.Full
member.summary:
PRAGMA synchronous = FULL — SQLite issues an fsync (or platform equivalent) on every commit, ensuring committed data survives a power failure or OS crash.
Significantly slower than for write-heavy workloads because every commit blocks until the OS confirms the data is on stable storage.

member.name: F:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.Models.SqliteSynchronousMode.Extra
member.summary:
PRAGMA synchronous = EXTRA — Like , but also syncs the directory containing the database file after deleting or truncating the rollback journal (DELETE/TRUNCATE mode). Provides the strongest durability guarantee against filesystems that do not persist directory entries on crash.
Has no additional benefit beyond in WAL mode.

member.name: M:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.SqliteConcurrencyExtensions.ExecuteWithRetryAsync``1(Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.DbContext,System.Func{Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.DbContext,System.Threading.Tasks.Task{``0}},System.Int32,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Executes an operation with automatic retry on SQLITE_BUSY and SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT errors.
member.param: The maximum number of retry attempts. Each retry waits using exponential backoff with jitter starting at 100 ms.

remarks.para: Two classes of busy error are handled:

list.item: SQLITE_BUSY / SQLITE_BUSY_RECOVERY / SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT — another connection holds a lock. The operation is retried after a backoff delay.

SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT — the connection's read snapshot became stale after another writer committed. The entire operation is restarted so that it can acquire a fresh snapshot. Any data read in the failed attempt must be re-queried inside the operation lambda.

remarks.para: SQLITE_LOCKED (same-connection conflict) is not retried and propagates immediately, as it indicates an application-level bug.

member.name: M:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.SqliteConcurrencyExtensions.SaveChangesSerializedAsync(Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.DbContext,System.Int32,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Saves all changes in the context while holding the shared per-database write lock, serializing concurrent writers at the application level before they contend in SQLite.
member.param: Maximum number of retry attempts if SQLITE_BUSY is returned even after the write lock is held. Uses exponential backoff starting at 50 ms, capped at 2 000 ms.
member.returns: The number of state entries written to the database.

remarks.para: Use this method instead of in background workers or other scenarios where multiple concurrent callers write to the same SQLite database. The shared lock ensures that at most one writer is active per database file at any point, avoiding SQLite-level busy-wait storms when many writers contend simultaneously.
If the calling code is already inside a (or any other scope that already holds the write lock), the method skips lock acquisition to prevent deadlocks.

member.name: M:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.SqliteConnectionEnhancer.PrepareForConnectionOpen(System.Data.Common.DbConnection)
member.summary: Prepares the database file for opening: clears the read-only file attribute and removes any stale .db-shm file. Must be called before the connection is opened so that SQLite sees a writable file and does not fall back to a read-only pager.

remarks.para: On Windows, MSBuild sometimes stamps the database file with when it is included in the project as Content with CopyToOutputDirectory. SQLite's sqlite3_open_v2 attempts O_RDWR; if the OS returns EACCES, it silently falls back to O_RDONLY, which permanently marks the pager as read-only. Any subsequent write attempt — including PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL — then returns SQLITE_READONLY. Clearing the attribute before the call to Open() prevents this fallback.

The .db-shm file is SQLite's shared-memory hash table that indexes WAL frames. It contains no committed data and is always recreated on the next WAL open. A stale copy left by a previous crashed process can cause SQLITE_READONLY_CANTINIT because SQLite detects a header mismatch.
This method runs at most once per database file per process (subsequent calls are no-ops). It is safe to call from multiple threads; an internal lock serializes the first call.

member.param: The connection that is about to be opened.

member.name: M:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.SqliteConnectionEnhancer.GetWalCheckpointStatusAsync(System.Data.Common.DbConnection,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Runs a passive WAL checkpoint and returns its status, which indicates whether the WAL is growing and whether long-running readers are blocking reclamation.
member.param: An open SQLite connection to the target database.
member.returns: A describing the current WAL state. Returns a zeroed status when the database is not in WAL mode.

remarks.para: A passive checkpoint transfers already-committed WAL frames to the main database file without blocking readers or writers. It is the safest checkpoint mode for health monitoring.

Call this periodically (e.g., every few minutes) to detect WAL growth pressure. A persistently result combined with a large means long-running read transactions are preventing WAL reclamation and will eventually degrade read performance as readers must scan an ever-larger WAL on every page lookup.

member.name: M:EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Concurrency.SqliteConnectionEnhancer.TryReleaseMigrationLockAsync(System.Data.Common.DbConnection,System.Boolean,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Checks for a stale EF Core migration lock and optionally removes it.
member.param: An open SQLite connection to the target database.
When (the default), deletes the stale lock row so that EF Core can proceed with migrations. When , only checks for the lock without modifying the database.

remarks.para: EF Core serializes concurrent migrations using a __EFMigrationsLock table. If a migration process crashes or is killed after acquiring the lock but before releasing it, subsequent migration attempts will block indefinitely waiting for a lock that will never be freed.

This is especially relevant in multi-instance deployments where every app instance calls Database.Migrate() at startup. The safest strategy is to run migrations as a single, controlled step (e.g. an init container or a deployment script) rather than from every instance concurrently. When a stale lock does occur, call this method once with set to before retrying the migration.
